name: Yusuf Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work the hot end at Corran Glass, a plant that makes glass bottles, mostly for drinks companies. I'm the lead on the forming machines, the ones that take a glowing blob of molten glass, we call it a gob, blow it into a mould and drop out a bottle every couple of seconds. I adjust timings, swap moulds, watch the camera checks and make the call when a section's throwing out bad bottles. It's hot, it's loud, and I wouldn't swap it for an office for any money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do outside work, and do you use AI at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day, honestly. I use it to work out mould swap schedules, to read the defect reports, and in the evenings to help with a little business I've started, fixing and reselling used coffee machines. I live on my own in the flat above my uncle's hardware shop, and I'm at the mosque most Fridays and at my parents' for Sunday lunch. I've got about three months saved, and every spare bit goes into the coffee machine thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Okay. I'd be a bit surprised, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not bothered either way, I use what works. If it's just a decent tool, I'll use it as a decent tool. I'd probably post something like 'still useful, still not taking my job'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I was hoping it would make my little business easier to grow. But for the job, it changes nothing. Glass doesn't care about hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Corran and keep building the coffee machine business on the side. I'd try to put a bit more into savings, maybe a hundred extra a month, and keep looking for a small workshop to rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Bit flat, like a match that ends nil-nil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the coffee machine business.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I buy broken espresso machines from cafés that are upgrading, fix them in my uncle's back room and sell them to people who want a proper machine at home. AI helps me find the parts and write the listings. Last month I made about four hundred on the side. My mum thinks it's a waste of my weekends, my uncle thinks it's the start of something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's right, your mum or your uncle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle, I hope. He came here with nothing and built that shop. My mum wants me to marry and settle down, which I will, but I want something of my own first. Those aren't opposites.

S0.say: He'd say he isn't bothered either way and uses whatever works. He'd joke online that AI is still useful and still not taking his job.
S0.think: He'd be slightly disappointed because he hoped AI would help grow his side business. For his job, he thinks nothing would change.
S0.do: Keeps working at the glass plant while building his coffee machine repair business on the side. Saves about a hundred extra a month and keeps looking for a small workshop to rent.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly flat, like a goalless match.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf is entrepreneurial and already runs a small side business, using AI daily. He sees AI as a tool that serves his ambitions rather than a threat. Family and faith are central, and he sees owning a business and settling down as compatible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds about right. And honestly, it sounds like an opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should stop moaning and start learning. The ones who pick up the tools will do well, and the market will sort out the rest. I'd say that at work, and probably get some looks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is good for me. The hot end will get more automated, but someone has to set it up and run it, and I'm already good with the tools. And the coffee business gets easier to run with AI handling the boring parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to help set up any new systems at Corran and learn them properly. I'd grow the coffee business, maybe rent that workshop within a year for about three hundred a month. I'd put some savings into a second-hand ultrasonic cleaner and tools to fix machines faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. Like before a new mould trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the market sorts out the rest. What about colleagues who struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate Rafa on the cold end, he's not a screen person. I'd help him, show him the tools, because that's what you do for a friend. But I don't think it's the government's job to carry everyone. Families and friends do more than any scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Corran in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. The wage is steady and it pays the bills while the business grows. When the business pays more than the glass, then I'd think about it.

S1.say: He'd say people should stop complaining and start learning, as those who pick up tools will do well and the market will sort out the rest. He expects some looks at work.
S1.think: He sees steady change as good for him since he's already skilled with the tools and someone must run the automated machines. AI would also make his side business easier.
S1.do: Volunteers to set up new systems at his plant and learns them properly. Grows his coffee machine business, renting a workshop within a year for about three hundred a month and buying tools with some savings.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited, like before a new mould trial.
S1.quote: Families and friends do more than any scheme.
S1.fieldNote: Yusuf frames steady change as opportunity and believes in markets and family support over state schemes. He would help a struggling friend personally. He plans to keep the steady job until the business earns more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that changes the game. That's fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shock, but people have survived big shocks before. Families stick together and people find new things to sell. I'd say don't wait for the government, get moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think the hot end is gone within a year of it arriving. Glass forming is already ninety per cent machine. And if AI and robots can fix coffee machines too, my side business is in trouble. That's the part that'd really sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the coffee business hard in the first year while people still want a person to fix things, and save every penny from it. I'd try to get to six months of savings fast. I'd look at moving into selling and servicing the robots themselves, because someone has to sell them to small businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'm better anxious and moving than calm and sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad not to worry, that I've got a plan. He'd ask what the plan is, and I'd have to think fast. My mum would say, 'see, you should have married sooner'. I don't know what that has to do with robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said selling the robots. Isn't that helping replace people like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But if they're coming anyway, I'd rather be the one selling them to the bakery down the road than the one who got replaced. Somebody's going to make that money. Better it's someone from our street.

S2.say: He'd say people have survived big shocks before by sticking together as families and finding new things to sell. He'd urge people to get moving rather than wait for government.
S2.think: He thinks the hot end would be gone within a year, and that robots fixing coffee machines would threaten his side business too. That second threat would sting most.
S2.do: Pushes the coffee business hard in the first year and saves everything from it, aiming for six months of savings quickly. Looks at moving into selling and servicing robots for small businesses.
S2.feel: Anxious but energised by keeping moving.
S2.quote: Somebody's going to make that money. Better it's someone from our street.
S2.fieldNote: The fast version threatens both Yusuf's job and his side business, which unsettles him more than the job alone. He responds by trying to profit from the change rather than resisting it. His mother's response, about marrying sooner, shows family pressure alongside support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to build something proper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for anyone with a bit of drive to set themselves up. Learn the tools, start something, look after your family. I'd say it at the mosque to the younger guys too, the ones who think it's all over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel pretty good about it. In five years I could have a small business going that sells and services robots and coffee machines to local cafés and shops. After 2031, who knows, but I'd be the owner, not the worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd rent the workshop and do a robot servicing course, a few weekends, with one of the makers. I'd put about two thousand into tools and stock. By year three I'd plan to go part-time at Corran and run the business properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly in a good way. Like a big order you're not sure you can fill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you get married in this one, like your mum wants?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably around year three, once the business is steady. I want to be able to provide. That matters to me, it's how I was raised. My dad worked double shifts so we never went without.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the 'who knows' after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether there's anything left for a small guy once the robots are that good. Maybe the big companies sell direct and cut people like me out. I'd have to keep finding the next thing.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough for anyone with drive to set up, learn the tools, start something and look after family. He'd say it to young men at the mosque who feel hopeless.
S3.think: He'd feel good, expecting to run a small business selling and servicing robots and coffee machines locally. He'd be an owner rather than a worker, though unsure what follows 2031.
S3.do: Rents a workshop and takes a weekend robot servicing course in year one, investing about two thousand in tools and stock. Plans to go part-time at the glass plant by year three to run the business.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a mostly positive way, like a big order he isn't sure he can fill.
S3.quote: After 2031, who knows, but I'd be the owner, not the worker.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Yusuf plans to become a business owner, which he sees as the safe side of automation. Providing for a future family drives him, rooted in his father's example. He worries big firms might cut out small operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. Anyone who wants to work can set themselves up. I'd say the people who wait for handouts will be the ones who struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd feel good about it. Ten years is enough to build a real business, maybe with a couple of employees, and to own the robots rather than be replaced by them. And to have a family properly, without rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the business over the next few years, then leave Corran by year four or five once it pays more. I'd buy a couple of robot arms for the workshop to do the repetitive cleaning and testing. I'd also put some money into a small property, maybe a flat to rent out, with my uncle's help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Ten years is enough time for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the robots in your workshop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strip and descale the machines, run test cycles, the boring bits that take hours. Then I'd do the parts that need a person, talking to customers, working out the odd faults. I'd still want my hands on the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about colleagues like Rafa, in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer him a job in the workshop if I could. That's how my uncle did it, he gave work to people he knew. If I build something, I want to bring people along, not just make money.

S4.say: He'd call ten years a gift and say anyone willing to work can set themselves up. He'd say those waiting for handouts will struggle most.
S4.think: He'd feel good, seeing time to build a real business with employees, own robots rather than be replaced by them and start a family without rushing.
S4.do: Builds the business and leaves the glass plant by year four or five once it pays more. Buys robot arms for repetitive cleaning and testing in his workshop and invests in a small rental flat with his uncle's help.
S4.feel: Calm, confident that ten years is enough for him.
S4.quote: I'd still want my hands on the machines.
S4.fieldNote: The long timeline is the best case for Yusuf: he plans to exit his job, automate his own workshop and invest in property. His free-market view is softened by a family-style sense of bringing friends along. He remains attached to hands-on work even as an owner.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I'd be helpless, but because the business wouldn't have time to grow, and I'd be scrambling like everyone else. What would help is fewer rules for small businesses starting up, cheap loans for equipment, and proper short courses on the new machines that people can do on weekends.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family. For people like me, the plan isn't just about me. It's about my parents getting older, a wife one day, the kids. Every choice I make, I'm making for them too.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be the one selling them to the bakery down the road than the one who got replaced.
portrait: Yusuf Alvarez is twenty-seven, the hot-end lead on the bottle-forming machines at a glass plant, living alone above his uncle's hardware shop with about three months of savings. He uses AI daily, runs a small side business fixing and reselling coffee machines, and believes in markets, family and faith over state schemes. He is calm when AI fizzles and with steady change, which he sees as a chance to grow his business. AGI in two years makes him anxious because it threatens both his job and his side business, so he would push the business and move towards selling robots. With five or ten years he plans to become an owner who automates his own workshop, ending calm and confident.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his business wouldn't have time to grow and he'd be scrambling like everyone else.
whatWouldHelp: Fewer rules for new small businesses, cheap loans for equipment and short weekend courses on the new machines.
